source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems
finding: Design: 75 students debugged a 4-bug Stata do-file in 20 minutes after a 10-minute tutorial. Each single bug was fixed by only about a fifth to a third or so of people.
numbers: N=75 (86 recruited, 11 dropped for poor English). 20 psychology, 24 computer science, 31 other majors. Bugs fixed per Table 5 totals: 28 (37.3%), 29 (38.7%), 25 (33.3%), 16 (21.3%) for the four bugs. Same condition for all; only backgrounds varied.
limits: Exploratory, one task, one language (Stata 7), no familiar-system control group (authors say so). The paper's Table 2 and Table 5 do not clearly agree on which bug has which count; the text says the valueofoutlier bug was found by nearly twice as many as the pvalues bug.
agent_relevance: The founding setup is small and single-task. Weigh its claims lightly, not as a law.

source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems
finding: Cluster analysis (Ward's method) of 132 behaviour measures, pooled into 22 groups, gave three comprehension strategies: depth-first information seekers (c1), inactive spec-and-output readers (c2), breadth-first inspect-everything guess-and-check (c3).
numbers: Cluster sizes 20 / 40 / 15. Over 33,000 coded actions; about 200 measures defined, 132 kept. The 3-cluster solution was chosen because more clusters only split the smallest group.
limits: Authors: 75 is small for clustering; comparing clusters on the measures that define them is dangerous; strategies depend on Stata-specific measures.
agent_relevance: Strategy labels came from the observer's measures, not from the person's plan. Do not treat them as stable types.

source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems
finding: Strategy tracked background, not skill at fixing: programming experience differed across clusters (p<.01), c3 highest. Only major and programming experience predicted cluster.
numbers: Programming experience (0-7): c1 2.52, c2 1.20, c3 3.59. Attitude to the experiment: 4.89 / 4.68 / 5.53 (p<.01). Computer attitude: 5.65 / 4.76 / 5.98.
limits: Self-reported experience; confounded with gender (3 of 24 CS majors were female).
agent_relevance: Strategy is a symptom of background. Changing the scaffold's strategy label will not change what the model knows.

source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems
finding: Strategy was not irrelevant: c2 and c3 fixed more bugs than c1 (p<.05), yet c2 (inactive) did as well as c3 (breadth-first). So no single strategy was best, but the depth-first one did worst overall.
numbers: Mean bugs fixed (0-4): c1 1.00 (SD .97), c2 1.65 (.98), c3 2.00 (1.07). Few people fixed more than 3 bugs. One bug (the one the paper calls valueofoutlier range) was fixed by 13 of 20 in c1, 12 of 40 in c2, 3 of 15 in c3 (chi-square p<.01).
limits: The headline 'no strategy was best' hides a c1 deficit: c1 chased one bug and ignored the rest.
agent_relevance: Depth-first tunnelling on one suspect costs bugs elsewhere. Checking all suspects before editing (S5 locate before fix) is cheap insurance, not a winning strategy.

source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems
finding: Bug-specific domain knowledge and attitude predicted success per bug. Math ability separated fixers of the valueofoutlier range bug; statistics knowledge and math ability separated fixers of the inverted axes bug. General verbal and problem-solving scores did not.
numbers: Valueofoutlier fixed vs not: self-rated math ability 5.07 vs 3.91, computer attitude 5.49 vs 4.82. Inverted axes fixed vs not: statistics test .40 vs .31, math ability 5.48 vs 4.41, computer attitude 5.83 vs 5.08. Problem-solving test .60 vs .59 and vocab .52 vs .54 for the first bug (no difference).
limits: Per-bug univariate comparisons on 75 people, many tests, no correction or effect sizes reported; the statistics test was near floor (mean about .34); several predictors are self-report.
agent_relevance: Relevant knowledge (here statistics and math) beat general ability and strategy. Retrieve domain facts about the likely bug type before choosing how to search.

source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems
finding: Surface cues steered attention. A comment that contradicted the code made one range bug far more findable than its twin without a comment; finding one often exposed the other. The longest command (a bug that changed no output) soaked up attention.
numbers: Text: nearly twice as many found the commented bug; those who found it were more likely to fix the twin. Fixers of the no-output for-loop bug spent less time on other lines and more on online-help examples.
limits: Discussion is interpretive; no controlled manipulation of the comment.
agent_relevance: Comments and big commands attract attention whether or not they matter. Inspecting real output is what cuts through (the inverted-axes bug needed graph inspection).

source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems
finding: Authors say the result contradicts expert-advantage-from-strategy studies in familiar systems (Gugerty and Olson; Nanja and Cook) and suggest strategy may matter more once the system is familiar.
numbers: A discussion claim, not a tested contrast: no familiar-vs-unfamiliar condition was run.
quote: as programmers become accustomed to a language and environment, comprehension strategy has a greater influence
limits: Hypothesis only.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the finding was observed in an unfamiliar system. For a model in a familiar language, strategy may matter more. Check on our own tasks.

source: Ko (2002) Honors thesis: Individual differences in programming, testing and debugging strategies in a statistical end-user programming environment
finding: The source thesis of Ko and Uttl: 86 participants did a programming task and a debugging task in Stata. Strategy clusters predicted success on the programming task, but not on the debugging task.
numbers: N=86 recruited. Programming task clusters (Table 17): cluster p1 (mostly CS majors) succeeded at generating random numbers in 34 of 41 cases; p2 in 1 of 23; p3 in 3 of 11. Debugging clusters d1/d2/d3 were related only to major and to fixing the valueofoutlier bug.
limits: Thesis, not peer reviewed. Table text was extracted from a PDF with a messy layout; check cell counts against the thesis before reuse.
agent_relevance: Strategy mattered when building new code (appropriate problem solving plus intelligence). It did not matter when debugging. Two tasks, two answers.

source: Ko (2002) Honors thesis: Individual differences in programming, testing and debugging strategies in a statistical end-user programming environment
finding: The thesis is stronger than the paper: programming experience, intelligence and statistics competence played no role in predicting debugging success; the structure of the program was the gatekeeper. The 2003 paper adds per-bug domain knowledge and attitude.
numbers: Thesis conclusion list on problem 2. Paper: see b05 for per-bug differences.
quote: Programming experience, along with intelligence and statistical competency played no role in predicting successful debugging
limits: Same data, different framing, different splits. The domain-knowledge claim is weaker in the thesis.
agent_relevance: Do not over-read 'domain knowledge predicts success'. The thesis points at the task (bug structure), not the person.

source: Ko (2002) Honors thesis: Individual differences in programming, testing and debugging strategies in a statistical end-user programming environment
finding: Thesis finding: those who inspected the program output first found more bugs, but few did. Trained programmers (CS majors) showed the same range of debug styles as psychology majors, and no style beat the others.
numbers: Three debugging styles: curious/distracted, hesitant/focused (few attempts), active/focused (changes everything, absorbs information). None was more successful.
limits: Observational; style classes from one task.
agent_relevance: Reading real output is the one behaviour that did separate people. A scaffold that forces output inspection before editing targets it.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching large language models to self-debug (ICLR 2024)
finding: Self-debugging gain depends on the information in the feedback, not on a clever procedure. Richer execution feedback gave more gain; code explanation alone helped mainly where no tests were available.
numbers: Spider (Codex): baseline 81.3, simple feedback 81.3, +explanation 84.1. TransCoder (Codex): baseline 80.4, simple 89.3, unit-test feedback 91.6, UT+explanation 92.5, UT+trace 87.9. MBPP (GPT-4): baseline 72.8, simple 78.8, UT 80.6, UT+expl 80.4, UT+trace 80.2. Without unit tests GPT-4 gained 3.6 on MBPP and about 1 elsewhere.
limits: Few-shot prompts. Numbers read from a PDF table with a messy column order; match the paper before quoting. Self-generated feedback left GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 overconfident.
agent_relevance: Real execution results are the knowledge that matters. Put actual run output into the loop; do not rely on the model judging its own code.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Without an outside signal, self-correction does not help and often hurts. With oracle labels the same loop improves a lot. So the gain comes from knowing the answer was wrong, not from the strategy.
numbers: GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7 over rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49 to 49 to 43. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, CSQA 89.7, HotpotQA 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5, CSQA 85.5, HotpotQA 59.0.
quote: the improvements vanish when oracle labels are not available
limits: Reasoning tasks, not code. 2023 models; small test sets (HotpotQA 100 items). Oracle setup is not a real deployment.
agent_relevance: A revise step needs an external check (tests, output, a fact lookup). Without one, keep it to one pass or drop it.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Self-repair is bottlenecked by the quality of the diagnosis text. Better feedback from a stronger model or a person lifts repair; the repair loop itself is secondary.
numbers: GPT-4 repair with GPT-4 feedback vs human feedback: overall 33.30% vs 52.60%; introductory 42.64 vs 62.21; interview 19.33 vs 45.67; competition 3.67 vs 14.67. 16 participants wrote 80 feedback items for 40 programs; GPT-4 feedback was inaccurate in 32 of 80, human in 7 of 80. When repair cost is counted, gains were modest or absent.
limits: Small human study (16 people, about an hour each, online); HumanEval and APPS; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as Ko and Uttl: the right piece of knowledge about the specific bug beats the procedure. Spend effort on an accurate diagnosis, such as a retrieved lesson or a test result.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents
finding: A fixed three-phase pipeline (localise, repair, validate) with no agent choosing its own strategy topped all open-source agents on SWE-bench Lite at lower cost.
numbers: 32.00% (96 of 300) resolved at $0.70 average cost. Compared in the paper's table: SWE-agent with GPT-4o 18.33% at $1.62; AutoCodeRover 19.00-21.67%; RAG baseline 2.67-4.33%. Resolve rate tracked share of patches at the correct location. Some closed commercial systems scored higher (e.g. 43.00%).
limits: SWE-bench Lite only; leaderboard from mid-2024; the authors removed leaked-patch and vague-issue items to build Lite-S.
agent_relevance: Free strategy did not buy accuracy; locating the fault correctly did. Supports a scripted locate-then-fix route over free wandering.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: agent-computer interfaces enable automated software engineering
finding: Same model, same tasks: interface design moved the score by several points. Tools that give exact, compact information beat tools that dump more.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite ablations (GPT-4 Turbo): default 18.0%; no edit command 10.3 (-7.7); iterative search 12.0 (-6.0); no search 15.7 (-2.3); summarized search 18.0; 100-line file viewer 18.0 vs 30-line 14.3 vs whole file 12.7. 51.7% of runs had at least one failed edit; chance of an eventual successful edit 90.5% overall but 57.2% after one failed edit.
limits: One main model family, 300-task subset; older results.
agent_relevance: Information quality in each step is the lever. Cap long outputs, give summaries, and re-localise after a failed edit.

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable automated debugging via LLM-driven scientific debugging (AutoSD)
finding: Forcing a human-like method (hypothesis, experiment with a real debugger, conclusion) kept repair accuracy near the plain LLM baseline. Its gains were explanation and a confidence signal, not accuracy.
numbers: Defects4J repairs: v1.2 LLM-Base 87 vs AutoSD 76; v2.0 110 vs 113. With real debugger output 73% of runs were plausible vs 63% when debugger output was model-imagined. Bugs with a plausible patch and a DONE signal: 89% correct. Human study, 20 people: accuracy better with explanations on 5 of 6 real bugs, time about equal.
limits: Defects4J and BugsInPy; 20 participants; no significance claimed for accuracy gain.
agent_relevance: Strategy choice (scientific method vs baseline) changed accuracy little. Real execution did (73 vs 63). A hypothesis trace helps trust, not score.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench: evaluating debugging capability of large language models
finding: Runtime feedback helps only some bug types: it helps syntax and reference errors and does not help, and can hurt, logic errors. Multiple and logic errors were hardest.
numbers: 4,253 instances, 18 bug types, C++/Java/Python; two commercial and four open models, zero-shot. Closed models below human level. Debugging and code-generation scores correlated for closed models.
limits: Bugs implanted by GPT-4 into LeetCode code, not real-world bugs.
agent_relevance: Fresh output is not enough. A logic bug needs a deeper diagnosis; tracebacks are too low-level. Give the specific wrong value.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) LDB: a large language model debugger via verifying runtime execution step-by-step
finding: Giving the model intermediate variable values per basic block (what human debuggers look at) improves repair over output-only feedback.
numbers: Improves baseline by up to 9.8% across HumanEval, MBPP and TransCoder (abstract figure).
limits: I read the abstract and parts of the text, not every table.
agent_relevance: Targeted runtime state is the useful knowledge about a bug. Supports a locate step with printed values.

source: Beller et al. (2018) On the dichotomy of debugging behavior among programmers (ICSE 2018)
finding: Real developers split on strategy (printf vs debugger), yet experience barely predicts which they use. Debugging is a small share of IDE time.
numbers: Survey of 176 developers; WatchDog field data on 723 IDE sessions (10.3 work years). Debugger run in 9% of sessions; debugging under 14% of active IDE time. No correlation between experience and use of IDE debugger or unit tests for debugging; weak correlation with hit counts; moderate with watches.
limits: Mostly Java users in Eclipse and IntelliJ; self-report plus IDE telemetry; no outcome measure of fix success.
agent_relevance: Another case where strategy is habit, not skill, and not tied to outcomes.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2021) An exploratory study of debugging episodes
finding: In live-streamed real work, long debugging episodes differed from short ones: slower first edit, more browsing and inspection, more outside resources. Half of episodes on reported defects did not end in a fix.
numbers: 11 professional developers, 15 sessions, 30 hours, 89 episodes. Reported defects 51 (+/-38) min, 5 of 10 unfixed. Self-inserted defects 6 (+/-8) min, 14% unfixed. Long episodes (>=12.3 min, n=23): 32 min, 62 activities, first edit at 3.2 min. Short (<1 min, n=23): 31 s, 4 activities, first edit at 6 s. Debugging 48% of session time (range 13-95%).
limits: Descriptive only, no inferential tests; small sample; one coder; live-stream effects. Read through a page-summarising tool, not the raw text.
agent_relevance: Hard bugs need information gathering before editing. A fast first edit marks an easy bug, not a good strategy. Do not reward speed to first edit.

source: Search for replications of Ko and Uttl (2003)
finding: Replication status: I found no direct replication of the three-strategy result and no later paper that re-tested 'domain knowledge beats strategy' in this form. The paper calls itself exploratory.
numbers: Checked: author PDF, the thesis, and papers found while searching. The web search quota ran out before a full forward-citation check.
limits: Absence is from limited searching; forward citations were not exhaustively checked.
agent_relevance: Treat as a single-study hint. Test it on our own tasks (strategy arm vs knowledge arm) before building on it.

source: Synthesis: Ko and Uttl (2003), Olausson (2024), Huang (2024)
finding: Cross-study pattern: three sources agree that the specific-knowledge term beats the procedure term. Human: bug-specific knowledge. LLM: accurate diagnosis (33.3% to 52.6% repair with better feedback) and an external check (oracle labels lift GSM8K from 75.9 to 84.3 for GPT-3.5).
numbers: Human N=75; LLM tests as in b12 and b13.
limits: Different domains (Stata debugging, code repair, reasoning). Consistency is suggestive, not proof.
agent_relevance: Design rule: spend scaffold effort on the information step (retrieve, run, check) before the procedure step.

source: Synthesis: Agentless, SWE-agent, benchmark quality
finding: Rival explanations for 'strategy matters little' in LLM agents: (1) information dominates, (2) benchmark noise and leaked patches hide strategy effects, (3) strong base models make a fixed pipeline enough. Agentless authors found benchmark flaws and built a filtered set.
numbers: Lite-S excludes issues that contain the exact ground-truth patch or are misleading; paper reports a result of 84 resolved (33.73%) on the filtered set.
limits: The authors of the simple method also built the filtered set; no independent check was done.
agent_relevance: Compare arms on a filtered, leak-free set and report intervals. Differences between strategies of a few points on 300 tasks are within noise.

source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems
finding: Boundary conditions: unfamiliar language and environment; 20-minute limit; short program with seeded bugs; novice-heavy sample; one statistics domain.
numbers: 20-minute limit, 4 seeded bugs, 2-hour sessions, think-aloud with no prompting, 10-minute tutorial.
limits: Seeded bugs are not natural; think-aloud may change behaviour.
agent_relevance: Our agent faces known languages and real tests. The finding may be weaker, or stronger, there.

source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems
finding: Methodological weakness: clusters were built from behaviour measures that also separate fixers from non-fixers on particular bugs (for example time spent on a command), so cluster-outcome links are partly circular.
numbers: Table 4 shows measures such as the valueofoutlier command being inspected separating fixers from non-fixers; the same kind of measures define the clusters (Fig. 5).
limits: Authors state that comparing clusters on their defining measures is dangerous; the consequence is my reading.
agent_relevance: Low confidence in 'strategy' as a clean variable. Prefer manipulated arms over observed clusters.

source: Synthesis: Chen et al. (2023) and Olausson et al. (2024), rival view
finding: Rival view: strategy matters when feedback is rich. In Self-Debug the plan is fixed and gain grows with feedback richness. This fits knowledge dominance, but also a strategy-by-information interaction; no study crosses both factors cleanly.
numbers: Self-Debug TransCoder (Codex): simple 89.3, UT 91.6, UT+expl 92.5. Olausson, counting cost, found gains modest or absent.
limits: Cross-paper reading, not one factorial experiment.
agent_relevance: Proposed test for us: 2x2 (fixed vs free strategy) x (execution feedback on vs off) on our debugging items.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent failure analysis
finding: Where agents fail: about half of unresolved runs (52.0%) were wrong or over-specific implementations; 23.4% were cascading failed edits. Successful runs finished early.
numbers: n=248 unresolved Lite instances classified by GPT-4o (87% agreement with authors on a labelled set). 93.0% of resolved runs submitted before the budget ran out vs 69.0% of all runs. Resolved: median 12 steps, $1.21; unresolved mean 21 steps, $2.52.
limits: LLM judge assigns categories; one agent configuration.
agent_relevance: Failure is mostly wrong diagnosis, not wrong procedure. Stop and re-diagnose rather than keep editing.

source: Synthesis: Beller et al. (2018) with Ko and Uttl (2003)
finding: Two independent human datasets, one lab (N=75) and one field (176 survey, 723 sessions), agree that experience level does not map neatly onto debugging strategy or success.
numbers: Lab: strategy linked to experience but weakly to success. Field: experience not correlated with debugger or test use.
limits: Different measures and populations; neither replicates the other.
agent_relevance: Treat 'expert strategy' as an unreliable thing to copy into the scaffold.
